warmup.q: A fourth node joins a three-node cluster with RF 3, streams its share and shows UN. What do the three old nodes do with the rows for ranges they no longer replicate?
options: Delete them as soon as the stream finishes
Keep them until someone runs nodetool cleanup on each old node
Drop them at their next routine compaction
Move them into the hints directory for the new node
warmup.why: Cassandra never deletes data just because ownership moved, and a normal compaction keeps every row it finds. In the Try-it the old nodes still held all 5,000 partitions after the join; nodetool cleanup, a special compaction, cut cass1 to 3,729. Hints are only for writes a down replica missed.

sections.h: A node is one JVM, four directories and two config files
sections.html:
Lesson 5 looked at a running Cassandra cluster from the inside. This case study builds one and runs it, and three ideas from earlier lessons do the work. Lesson 3's rebalancing decides which ranges move when a node joins or leaves, and who starts the move. Lesson 2's token ring with 16 tokens per node decides what those ranges are. And the catch-up tools of leaderless replication, hints and anti-entropy repair from the Replication track, keep copies equal while nodes come and go.

A Cassandra node is one Java process, org.apache.cassandra.service.CassandraDaemon, plus the files it owns. Everything an operator does, from setup to backups, comes down to those files and to the few settings that tie one process to the others.

You install two things: a JDK and Cassandra. As of November 2026 the latest GA release is 5.0.9, from August 2026, and the labs pin it; 6.0 is in alpha (section 3 says what it changes). The 5.0 docs ask for Java 11 or 17, and the cassandra:5.0.9 image ships Temurin 17. Cassandra comes as a tarball from the downloads page (bin/, conf/, lib/), as Debian and RPM packages, or as the Docker image the labs use; cqlsh needs Python 3. In the image, /etc/cassandra holds the configuration, /var/lib/cassandra the data and /var/log/cassandra the logs.

The data directory has four parts, and each one is a mechanism you have already met:

  • commitlog/ is the write-ahead log from the write path in the Data models track's wide-column lesson: 32 MiB segments, recycled once their writes are flushed.
  • data/ has one directory per keyspace and inside it one per table, such as payments/ledger-a0d7ae60..., holding the SSTables. snapshots/ and backups/ appear in there later.
  • hints/ keeps writes for replicas that are down (the Replication track's hints), one file per target node.
  • saved_caches/ holds the key cache, saved every 4 hours, so a restarted node doesn't start cold.

The commit log is written sequentially and fsynced; SSTables are read at random places. On spinning disks the two needed separate disks. On SSDs one volume works, but the commit log still competes with compaction for bandwidth. data_file_directories can list several disks, and Cassandra splits the token ranges between them.

Memory has two users: the JVM heap, and the operating system's page cache (from the Operating systems track's page cache lesson), which serves SSTable reads from RAM. If you don't set the heap, cassandra-env.sh takes half the machine's RAM, up to 31 GB with the G1 collector the image uses. Inside a container that rule misfires. The script asks free how much memory there is, and free reports the Docker VM's 7.75 GB, not the container's 1 GB limit (cgroups, from the Operating systems track's lesson on containers). The lab nodes get -Xmx320M only because the Compose file sets MAX_HEAP_SIZE, and even so the Try-it shows -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=1983M, a quarter of the VM, for a container limited to 1 GB. Set the heap yourself, always, and leave the rest of the RAM to the page cache. A node that goes over its container's limit is killed by the kernel and exits with code 137.

sections.h: cassandra.yaml: the few settings that turn nodes into a cluster
sections.html:
The cassandra.yaml in the 5.0.9 image has 2,485 lines, and almost all of them can stay as they are. A new node has to answer a handful of questions before it can join a cluster, and each answer is a setting.

Which cluster is this? cluster_name. Gossip drops every message from a node with a different name (the receiver logs ClusterName mismatch), so a test node pointed at production by mistake can't join it. The node also saves the name on its first start and refuses to start if the file says something else later.

Whom do I ask first? seeds, under seed_provider: two or three stable nodes per datacenter, the same list on every node, never a node joining for the first time (lesson 5).

Which address? listen_address is the one other nodes connect to, on storage_port 7000. rpc_address and native_transport_port 9042 are for clients. The file says setting listen_address to 0.0.0.0 "is always wrong". rpc_address may be 0.0.0.0, but then broadcast_rpc_address has to tell drivers the real address; the image's start script does exactly that. Behind NAT, broadcast_address is what other nodes are told.

Where am I? endpoint_snitch: GossipingPropertyFileSnitch plus dc= and rack= in cassandra-rackdc.properties. The default, SimpleSnitch, puts every node in datacenter1 and rack1, and the production docs say changing racks after provisioning isn't supported.

How many tokens? num_tokens: 16 with allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor set to your replication factor. Both apply only at a node's first start. The production docs suggest 4 tokens for clusters expected to grow past 30 nodes and advise against 16 above 50.

Where does data go? data_file_directories, commitlog_directory, hints_directory and saved_caches_directory. They're commented out in the file and default to $CASSANDRA_HOME/data, which the image links to /var/lib/cassandra.

How safe is an acknowledged write on one node? commitlog_sync: periodic with commitlog_sync_period: 10000ms: the node acknowledges before it fsyncs and fsyncs every 10 seconds, so a power cut on one machine can lose its last 10 seconds of writes. The other replicas still have them, which is one more reason RF 3 isn't optional. batch and group wait for the fsync before acknowledging and pay for it in latency.

Last, keyspaces. CREATE KEYSPACE payments WITH replication = {'class': 'NetworkTopologyStrategy', 'dc1': 3} names a datacenter, and the name must match what the snitch reports, letter for letter. The docs say production clusters should never use SimpleStrategy, and that includes the system keyspaces: describecluster shows system_auth on SimpleStrategy with one copy, so losing one node can lock everyone out once authentication is on. Alter it to NetworkTopologyStrategy with 3 copies per datacenter, then repair it.

sections.h: Adding and removing nodes: who streams which ranges
sections.html:
When cass4 joined the lab cluster, it received 276, 300 and 280 KiB from the three old nodes, and none of them deleted anything. Adding a node is the slowest routine job in Cassandra, because data has to move before the new node can serve it, and every step of a join exists to keep reads and writes correct while it moves. In lesson 3's terms, Cassandra rebalances by splitting: cass4's 16 new tokens cut slices off existing ranges, so it takes a little from every node. And the rebalancing is manual: nothing moves until an operator starts a node or runs a command, so a node that is down for an hour never triggers a move.

  1. cass4 starts with the same cluster_name and seeds, empty data directories, and its own address not in the seed list, so it will bootstrap.
  2. It learns the map from a seed and waits until it has the schema (JOINING: waiting for ring information, then schema complete, ready to bootstrap).
  3. It picks 16 tokens with the allocator and announces them in gossip with a BOOT status. The others now show it as UJ, up and joining. From this moment, coordinators send cass4 a copy of every new write for the ranges it is about to own, so nothing written during the stream is missed.
  4. It sleeps ring_delay, 30 seconds, so the whole cluster has heard.
  5. It streams. With 16 tokens and RF 3, cass4 becomes a replica of 47 ranges, and it takes each range from the replica it replaces: the node that held that range before and won't afterwards. Cassandra insists on that source (cassandra.consistent.rangemovement, true by default), so the three new copies hold exactly what the three old ones held. Copying from another replica could lose a write: one that only the departing node and one other had acknowledged would end up on one node, and the quorum overlap from the Replication track would be gone. cass4 logs one Bootstrap: range ... exists on ... line per range, and the lab checks its model against all 47.
  6. It switches to NORMAL and shows UN.

That took 90 seconds here; real nodes take hours, and the worked example sizes one. Join one node at a time and wait for UN, because two joins at once would each compute their ranges against a ring that is about to change.

The old nodes keep everything. Cassandra doesn't delete data for ranges a node no longer owns, so their Load stayed at 1.16 MiB. nodetool cleanup on each old node rewrites its SSTables without those ranges: cass1 went from 5,000 partitions to 3,729. Run it on every old node after the last new node has joined, one node at a time, because it is a compaction and costs disk I/O.

Removing a node runs the film backwards. nodetool decommission, run on the live node, marks it LEAVING, streams each of its ranges and its hints to the new owners, and leaves: cass4 sent 7 SSTables to each of the three. A dead node can't stream, so nodetool removenode <host ID> makes the surviving replicas stream for it, and -Dcassandra.replace_address_first_boot=<dead address> lets a new machine take over the dead node's tokens. If the dead node was down longer than max_hint_window, run repair afterwards.

Steps 2 to 4 lean on gossip. cass4 announces its tokens and sleeps 30 seconds in the hope that every node has heard, and for a moment two nodes can disagree about who owns a range. Cassandra 6.0, in alpha since April 2026, replaces the hope with a log. Its Transactional Cluster Metadata (CEP-21) turns membership, token ownership and schema into entries of one log, ordered by consensus in a Cluster Metadata Service (CMS) on a few nodes. Each entry gets the next epoch number, and every node applies them in epoch order. A join is a series of entries, and before each next step the joining node waits until the other nodes acknowledge the last epoch, a progress barrier. Here a second 6.0-alpha2 node, started by hand, joins a one-node cluster (log trimmed):

Committing REGISTER
Committing PREPARE_JOIN
Committing START_JOIN
Collected acknowledgements from [/172.24.0.2:7000, /172.24.0.3:7000] ... progress barrier for epoch Epoch{epoch=6} at EACH_QUORUM
Committing MID_JOIN
Collected acknowledgements from [/172.24.0.2:7000, /172.24.0.3:7000] ... progress barrier for epoch Epoch{epoch=7} at EACH_QUORUM
Committing FINISH_JOIN
NORMAL

No 30-second sleep: the join took half a second, and the log then held those steps as epochs 4 to 8. A cluster upgraded from 5.0 keeps gossip-held metadata until every node runs 6.0 and an operator runs nodetool cms initialize. 6.0 also brings Accord, opt-in transactions across partitions, which the Transactions track runs.

try.title: Add cass4, clean up, then decommission it
steps: Give the cluster something to move: 50,000 ledger rows (about a minute), then flush every node so nodetool status counts the data as Load. COPY may print a WriteTimeout ... will retry later or two on a busy laptop; it retries them. Check nodetool status payments: every node owns 100%.

Start cass4, which the Compose file keeps behind a profile: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml --profile grow up -d cass4. Run nodetool status payments on cass1 every 20 seconds or so: predict the letters cass4 shows, then its Owns, and whether the old nodes' Load changes. When cass4 is UN, read its log.
Run nodetool cleanup payments on cass1, cass2 and cass3, one after the other, and compare the partition counts before and after. Wait a minute and check the Load column again: it travels by gossip.

Decommission cass4 (about 70 seconds), read its log, check nodetool status, then remove the container: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml --profile grow rm -sfv cass4. Leave the three nodes running for the next Try-it.

Optional, about 2 GB and two minutes: start one Cassandra 6.0-alpha2 node with docker compose -f env/cassandra6.yml up -d --wait (the Transactions track uses the same file), print its Cluster Metadata Service and its metadata log, then stop it with docker compose -f env/cassandra6.yml down -v.

sections.h: Day two: nodetool, repair, drain and snapshots
sections.html:
nodetool is how an operator talks to a node. It's a JMX client, and by default a node accepts JMX only on localhost, port 7199, which is why every Try-it runs it inside a container with exec. Five commands cover most days:

  • status: UN everywhere, or a DN, UJ or UL that shouldn't be there?
  • describecluster: one schema version?
  • tablestats <keyspace.table>: SSTable count, read and write latency, Maximum tombstones per slice (the wide-column lesson's tombstones), and Compacted partition maximum bytes against the 100 MB guideline.
  • compactionstats: pending tasks. A number that keeps growing means compaction is falling behind the writes, and reads slow down as SSTables pile up.
  • tpstats: pending and blocked work per thread pool, and dropped messages. When an earlier, faster version of the ledger load hit the three small nodes, cass1 dropped 87,398 MUTATION_REQ messages, writes it gave up on because they waited past the write timeout. Hints and repair put them back.

Repair is the one job Cassandra never starts by itself, and it has a deadline. Hints cover 3 hours of downtime and read repair covers the keys someone reads; everything else drifts until nodetool repair compares Merkle trees range by range (the Replication track's anti-entropy). Deletes make it urgent: a replica that misses a tombstone for longer than gc_grace_seconds, 10 days by default, can bring the row back. Plain nodetool repair is incremental: it compares only data written since the last incremental repair and then marks it repaired. --full compares everything. The docs suggest incremental every 1 to 3 days and full every 1 to 3 weeks, and at the very least every node within 7 days while gc_grace_seconds is 10 days. A run repairs every range the node holds, so running it on all nodes repairs each range RF times; -pr limits each run to the node's primary ranges, and then you run it on every node. --preview estimates what would stream without streaming: in the Try-it, two writes that cass3 missed showed up as 3 mismatching ranges.

Restart one node at a time, and drain it first. nodetool drain stops client traffic, announces the shutdown in gossip (so peers mark the node down at once instead of waiting 20 seconds for phi), and flushes every memtable. The restart then has nothing to replay: Log replay complete, 0 replayed mutations in 68 ms. A rolling restart is drain, restart, wait for UN on every node, then the next node. With RF 3 and QUORUM, one node down at a time never blocks a range.

Backups start with nodetool snapshot. It flushes and hard-links every SSTable of the keyspace into snapshots/<tag>/, next to a schema.cql that recreates the table. A hard link (from the Operating systems track's file systems lesson) is a second name for the same inode, so a snapshot takes no time and no extra disk until compaction deletes the originals, which the snapshot then keeps alive. incremental_backups: true, or nodetool enablebackup, hard-links every newly flushed or streamed SSTable into backups/. Neither is a backup until it's copied off the node; after that, clear it (nodetool clearsnapshot) or it fills the disk. To restore, sstableloader streams the files into a live cluster, or you copy them into the table's directory and run nodetool import.

sections.h: A second datacenter, and a production checklist
sections.html:
In the Try-it, a read at LOCAL_ONE in the new datacenter returned 0 rows for a ledger entry that existed. The keyspace already said 'dc2': 1; nobody had copied the data to dc2 yet. That gap is the hard part of adding a datacenter.

A second datacenter is for a region outage, for users far from the first region, or for analytics kept off the payment nodes. Each datacenter holds full copies with its own replication factor, and clients stay local: LOCAL_QUORUM waits for a majority in the coordinator's datacenter only, so a cross-region round trip of about 70 ms never sits on the write path. The remote datacenter still gets every write, in the background: the coordinator sends one copy to a node there, and that node forwards it to the other replicas in its datacenter.

The procedure, as the Try-it ran it:

  1. Start the new nodes with dc=dc2, the same cluster name and seeds, and auto_bootstrap: false, so they join the ring without streaming. They own 0% of payments.
  2. ALTER KEYSPACE payments to add 'dc2' (3 in production), and do the same for system_auth, system_distributed and system_traces.
  3. On each new node, nodetool rebuild -- dc1 streams that node's dc2 replicas from dc1: about 1.2 MiB from three nodes here.
  4. Only then send the region's clients to dc2: the Java driver's basic.load-balancing-policy.local-datacenter = dc2.

Leave auto_bootstrap at its default and the new node streams some ranges as it joins, after which rebuild refuses with Discovered existing bootstrap data ...; aborting bootstrap.

Most of a production checklist is decided before the first node starts, because the cluster name, tokens, snitch and racks can't be changed in place later. The rest is routine that has to happen on a calendar, or it doesn't happen at all.

Area Do this Because
Topology 3 racks per datacenter (one per availability zone), the same number of nodes in each NetworkTopologyStrategy puts one copy per rack; a smaller rack's nodes carry more
Before first start cluster_name, GossipingPropertyFileSnitch, dc and rack, num_tokens (16, or 4 past about 30 nodes), the allocator set to your RF none of these can change in place later
Seeds 2 or 3 per datacenter, the same list on every node, never a joining node a seed never bootstraps
Keyspaces NetworkTopologyStrategy, 3 per datacenter, system keyspaces included system_auth starts with one copy
Clients LOCAL_QUORUM reads and writes, the driver's local datacenter set quorums overlap without a cross-region wait
Memory MAX_HEAP_SIZE set explicitly, the rest of RAM left to the page cache the default reads the host's RAM, not a container's limit
Time NTP on every node and every client last write wins by timestamp (the Replication track's concurrent writes lesson)
Security authentication, authorization and TLS between nodes and to clients, from day one the defaults let anyone in; adding encryption later risks downtime
Changes one node at a time and wait for UN; cleanup after adding; drain before restarting ranges move against a stable ring; old data stays until cleanup
Repair incremental every 1 to 3 days, full every 1 to 3 weeks, every node within gc_grace_seconds deleted rows come back after 10 days
Backups snapshots and incremental backups copied off the node, cleared after, restore tested a hard link on the same disk dies with the disk
Monitoring node states, dropped messages, pending compactions, hints, p99 latency per table they move before users notice

refs.title: Apache Cassandra 5.0: adding a datacenter with auto_bootstrap: false (topology changes)

analogy: Think of a team of three clerks who each keep a full copy of the account files. When a fourth clerk is hired, the manager assigns them a share of the alphabet, and for each letter they copy the files from the one colleague who is handing that letter over. The old clerks don't shred anything on the day; each one shreds the letters they gave away when someone tells them to (cleanup). When a clerk leaves, they hand each letter back to whoever takes it over. A clerk who disappeared can't hand anything over, so the colleagues who kept copies do it instead (removenode). The analogy breaks on the shredding: a real clerk would notice they still hold files that aren't theirs, while a Cassandra node keeps them forever, counts them in its disk usage, and can even serve them again if the ranges move back.
world: Running Cassandra next to your payments services looks a lot like running Oracle with Data Guard, minus the DBA's single primary: every node is the same, and the runbook is a sequence of nodetool commands, one node at a time. Put that runbook in code. On Kubernetes, an operator such as cass-operator runs these steps for you, but you still choose the racks (one per availability zone), the heap, the tokens and the repair schedule. Set the heap explicitly in the pod spec; the default reads the node's RAM, not the pod's limit, and an OOM-killed pod exits with 137 in the middle of a compaction. Schedule repair like a settlement batch, with an alert when it hasn't completed within 7 days, because a missed repair shows up only 10 days later, as deleted payments coming back. And send your Quarkus services in each region to their own datacenter with LOCAL_QUORUM, so a slow link to the other region never adds 70 ms to a payment authorization.
mistake: The most common mistake is adding nodes and never running nodetool cleanup. The cluster looks healthy: every node is UN, Owns adds up, and the new nodes serve their ranges. Nobody notices that the old nodes' disks didn't shrink, until a disk fills during a big compaction. Worse, if ranges ever move back to an old node, a decommission for example, it serves its stale copies again, including rows deleted since, whose tombstones may already be gone. People skip it because the join ended with "state jump to NORMAL", which sounds like the end. The fix is to make cleanup part of adding capacity: after the last new node is UN, run nodetool cleanup on each old node, one at a time, and check that Load drops to roughly its new Owns share.

compare.title: Taking a node out: decommission or removenode

a.label: nodetool decommission (the node is alive)
a.title: nodetool decommission (the node is alive)
a.html: # run ON the node that leaves nodetool decommission # LEAVING: sleeping 30000 ms ... # LEAVING: streaming data to other nodes <- it sends its own data # LEAVING: streaming hints to other nodes # Announcing that I have left the ring # DECOMMISSIONED

b.label: nodetool removenode (the node is dead)
b.title: nodetool removenode (the node is dead)
b.html: # run on ANY live node, with the dead node's host ID nodetool status # DN ... 3af36864-e701-... nodetool removenode 3af36864-e701-442b-862a-96cb9bb04775 nodetool removenode status # the surviving replicas stream to the new owners; # the dead node's copy is simply gone

compare.note: Both end with the node's tokens off the ring and its ranges owned by others. Decommission is the clean path: the leaving node sends exactly what it held, including its hints, while it's still a full replica. Removenode is for a node that can't take part, so the data comes from the other replicas, and anything only the dead node had (a write acknowledged at ONE, a hint it was holding) is lost unless repair finds it elsewhere. If the machine is coming back as a replacement, replace_address_first_boot is better than either: the new node takes the dead one's tokens and nobody else's ranges move.

worked.title: Plan growing a six-node payments cluster to nine

steps.say: Write down what you have and what the new layout will be. Grow every rack by one node, so racks stay equal.
steps.code:
now     6 nodes, RF 3, racks a/b/c with 2 nodes each, 600 GB per node
after   9 nodes, racks a/b/c with 3 nodes each
per node after: 600 GB x 6 / 9 = 400 GB

steps.say: Estimate the stream for one new node. Each source is throttled by stream_throughput_outbound, 24 MiB/s by default, and a node streams from several sources at once.
steps.code:
data to receive     about 400 GB
sources             about 3, at 24 MiB/s each = 72 MiB/s
time                400 x 1024 MiB / 72 MiB/s = 5,689 s, about 1.6 h
three nodes, one at a time: about 5 h

steps.say: Add them one at a time, one per rack, and check each before the next. Don't clean up in between: the next join would move ranges again.
steps.code: for each new node (rack a, then b, then c): start it (not in its own seed list, same cluster_name, its rack in rackdc) nodetool status # UJ ... then UN nodetool netstats # streams finished, nothing pending

steps.say: Clean up the six old nodes. Cleanup is a compaction that rewrites everything the node holds, throttled by compaction_throughput, 64 MiB/s in 5.0.9's yaml.
steps.code:
per old node   600 x 1024 MiB / 64 MiB/s = 9,600 s, about 2.7 h
six nodes      one at a time about 16 h; one per rack at a time about 5.3 h
after          Load about 400 GB, Owns about 33.3% on all nine

steps.say: Finish with a repair of the keyspace, so any write a new node missed while it streamed is reconciled, and record the new layout in the runbook.
steps.code: for n in all nine: nodetool repair -pr payments nodetool status payments # 9 x UN, Owns about 33.3% each nodetool describecluster # one schema version

lab.title: Model token-range movement and check it against the real cluster
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed: the tests read nodetool ring, describering and cass4's stream log, captured from the Try-it and kept in src/test/resources/sfz/shard/l06/. Five of eight fail with NotImplementedError. The three that pass check the given Ring against the real cluster: its replica walk matches describering range by range, and its owns matches the Owns column of nodetool status.

Write bootstrapSources: for each range cass4 replicates after the join, its old replicas, its new replicas, and the one old replica that isn't a new one. Two tests pass, including the one that compares you with the 47 Bootstrap: range ... exists on ... lines cass4 logged.
Write cleanup: for each range of the new ring, the old replicas that aren't replicas any more. The test checks that each old node deletes exactly what it streamed away.
Write decommissionTargets: for each range the leaving node replicates, the replica that appears once it's gone. All eight pass, including the one that hands every range back to the node it came from.

Experiment: in bootstrapSources, stream every range from the first old replica (the primary) instead. The test against the real log fails: Cassandra picks the replica being replaced, not the closest one. Put it back.
hints: Every range of the new ring sits inside exactly one range of the old ring, because the old tokens are a subset of the new ones. So before.replicasOf(range.end) gives the old replicas of a new range.
old - new.toSet() keeps the order of old. With RF 3 and three old nodes it has exactly one element; .singleOrNull() ?: old.first() covers small clusters.
getOrPut(node) { linkedSetOf() } += range builds a map of sets in one line, and sortedMapOf keeps the output stable.
For decommission, compare ring.replicas(range) with ring.withoutNode(leaving).replicasOf(range.end); the new name in the second list receives the range.

drill.title: The node-change runbook, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the commands, in order, to (1) add cass4 to a three-node RF-3 cluster, (2) later retire cass2, which is healthy, and (3) deal with cass3, whose disk died and won't come back. After each command, write what you check before going on.

answer.html: # 1. add cass4: same cluster_name and seeds, not its own seed, empty data dirs start cass4 nodetool status # UJ, then UN; Owns about 75% each nodetool cleanup # on cass1, cass2, cass3, one at a time nodetool tablestats ... # partitions and Load drop to about 75% # 2. retire cass2 (alive): it streams its own ranges away nodetool decommission # run ON cass2 nodetool status # cass2 gone, others UN; no cleanup needed # 3. cass3 is dead: the survivors stream for it nodetool status # DN ... <host ID of cass3> nodetool removenode <host ID> # on any live node nodetool removenode status # until no removals in process nodetool repair -pr # on every node, in case cass3 held the only copy of something # or: start a new machine with -Dcassandra.replace_address_first_boot=<cass3's address>

recap: A node is one JVM plus commitlog/, data/, hints/ and saved_caches/. Set the heap yourself, and get cluster_name, seeds, addresses, the snitch with dc and rack, num_tokens and the allocator right before the first start; keyspaces use NetworkTopologyStrategy, system keyspaces included.

A joining node picks tokens, gossips them, sleeps 30 seconds and streams each new range from the replica it replaces; old nodes keep their copies until nodetool cleanup. Nothing moves unless an operator starts it.
Decommission streams a live node's data away; removenode makes the survivors stream for a dead one; replace_address_first_boot takes over a dead node's tokens.
Repair every node within gc_grace_seconds (incremental often, full every 1 to 3 weeks), drain before every restart, one node at a time, and copy snapshots off the node.
A new datacenter starts with auto_bootstrap: false, gets replicas with ALTER KEYSPACE, and serves clients only after nodetool rebuild, or LOCAL_* reads come back empty.

5.0.9 is the current GA release. 6.0 (alpha) moves membership, tokens and schema into a metadata log ordered by consensus, so a join is a series of epochs every node applies in the same order; it also adds Accord transactions.

explain.prompt: Your manager asks: "We need more capacity for the holiday peak. What exactly happens when we add a Cassandra node, how long will it take, and what do we have to do afterwards?" Answer in a few sentences.
explain.answer: We start the new node with the same cluster name and seeds and its rack set, and it isn't a seed itself, so it bootstraps. It learns the ring from a seed, picks 16 tokens with the allocator so load stays even, and announces them; from then on it gets a copy of every new write for its future ranges. After 30 seconds it streams each of its ranges from the replica it's replacing. That's the long part: at the default 24 MiB/s per source, about 400 GB takes over an hour and a half per node, so for three nodes we plan most of a day, adding one at a time and waiting for each to show UN. Afterwards we run nodetool cleanup on every old node, one at a time, because Cassandra doesn't delete the data they handed over; without it their disks stay full. Then a repair, a check that every node owns about the same share, and an update to the runbook. None of it needs downtime: with RF 3 and LOCAL_QUORUM, payments keep flowing throughout.

deeper.html:
Streaming has two modes. When an SSTable lies entirely inside the ranges being moved, Cassandra 4.0 and later can send the whole file without decoding it (zero-copy, entire-SSTable streaming, throttled by entire_sstable_stream_throughput_outbound). With 16 vnodes per node, a joining node's ranges are small slices of every SSTable, so most streaming decodes each SSTable and sends only the partitions in range, throttled by stream_throughput_outbound, 24 MiB/s by default. nodetool setstreamthroughput changes the limit on a running node; raise it for a planned expansion at night, lower it if streaming hurts client latency.

nodetool netstats shows streams in progress, per peer and per file, during a bootstrap, decommission, rebuild or repair; on the lab's tiny data set they finished between two calls, but on real clusters it's the command you watch. nodetool removenode status and nodetool decommission (which blocks until done) are the others.

Incremental repair splits SSTables into repaired and unrepaired sets, and compaction keeps the two apart, which is how Percent repaired in tablestats is measured. A full repair ignores the split. Tools such as Cassandra Reaper schedule repairs in small token sub-ranges across the cluster so that no single run takes hours; whatever runs it, alert when a node hasn't completed a repair within 7 days.

nodetool assassinate exists, and its help text says what it is: forcefully remove a dead node without re-replicating any data, as a last resort when removenode can't work. Data that lived only on that node is gone.

For restores, nodetool import loads SSTables you've copied into a table's directory on a live node, and sstableloader streams them to whichever nodes own them now, so it works even when the ring has changed since the snapshot. Restoring a whole cluster from snapshots is easiest when the new cluster has the same tokens: put each old node's tokens in the new node's initial_token before its first start.
